gallery.title: File:AllendeMeteorite.jpg
gallery.description: A 520g individual of the Allende meteorite shower. Allende is a carbonaceous chondrite (CV3) that fell on 1969 February 8 in Mexico. This specimen is approx. 8 centimeters wide. Note the patches of dull black fusion crust. Severals condrules and CAIs can be seen embedded in the gray matrix.

gallery.title: File:Allende meteorite, crusted individual, 5g.jpg
gallery.description: Allende meteorite, fresh crusted individual. It was almost certainly recovered shortly after the fall occurred on Feb 8th 1969, in Chihuahua, Mexico.  This meteorite is classified as a CV3 (Vigarano group, type 3) carbonaceous chondrite. Specimen weighs 5 grams. Note the contraction cracks in the fusion crust which formed when the stone rapidly cooled during it's descent through the atmosphere.

gallery.title: File:Allende meteorite, carbonaceous chondrite (14787764392).jpg
gallery.description:
Allende meteorite, carbonaceous chondrite.

Allende has small, spherical to subspherical structures called chondrules (all chondrites have these). Allende also contains whitish, irregularly-shaped patches called CAIs (“calcium-aluminum inclusions”), composed of high-temperature Ca-Al-Ti silicates & oxides. The blackish, fine-grained, carbon-rich matrix consists of Fe-olivine & poorly graphitized carbon. A few tiny specks of metallic iron-nickel alloy also occur. Allende rocks represent the near-oldest meteoritic material known. The olivine chondrules in Allende rocks date to 4.560 billion years. The CAIs in Allende rocks date to 4.568 billion years.

gallery.title: File:Carbonaceous chondrite (Allende Meteorite) (4.560-4.568 Ga) 5 (16763229093).jpg
gallery.description:
Carbonaceous chondrite - large slice (549 grams) of the Allende Meteorite. (Maine Mineral & Gem Museum collection, Bethel, Maine, USA)
Carbonaceous chondrites are dark gray to blackish-colored chondrite meteorites with a relatively carbon-rich matrix.  The first large sampling of carbonaceous chondrites available to meteoriticists came with the 1969 fall of the Allende Meteorite.  Before Allende, carbonaceous chondrite material was exceedingly rare.  Allende has become the most heavily studied and the most famous carbonaceous chondrite.
Allende impacted on Earth at 1:05 AM on 8 February 1969.  Its known strewn field trends southwest-to-northeast in the vicinity of the town of Allende in southeastern Chihuahua State, northern Mexico.
The slice shown above displays the internal structure & composition of the Allende carbonaceous chondrite.  Allende has small, spherical to subspherical structures called chondrules (all chondrites have these).  Allende also contains whitish, irregularly-shaped patches called CAIs (“calcium-aluminum inclusions”), composed of high-temperature Ca-Al-Ti silicates & oxides.  The blackish, fine-grained, carbon-rich matrix consists of Fe-olivine & poorly graphitized carbon.  A few tiny specks of metallic iron-nickel alloy also occur.

Allende rocks represent the near-oldest meteoritic material known.  The olivine chondrules in Allende rocks date to 4.560 billion years.  The CAIs in Allende rocks date to 4.568 billion years.

gallery.filename: Fragments de la météorite Allende, chondrite carbonée, Muséum national d'histoire naturelle.jpg
gallery.title: File:Fragments de la météorite Allende, chondrite carbonée, Muséum national d'histoire naturelle.jpg
gallery.description:
Allende. Chondrite carbonée CV3 (632 et 421 g). Chihuahua, Mexique. Tombée le 8 février 1969. Galerie de minéralogie du Muséum national d'histoire naturelle de Paris (France).
Légende lors de l'exposition "Trésors de la terre" : "Les objets blancs que l'on peut voir dans cette météorite primitive ont été formés en même temps que le Soleil, et c'est en mesurant leur âge que l'on peut déterminer celui du Soleil : 4,568 milliards d'années."
